metadata.prompt:
[Intro | harpsichord alone plays the album's motif fast and hard, deliberately, in 12/8]
[Gigue | band crashes in at 176 BPM, galloping compound rhythm, B minor, exhilarating]
[Unison | harpsichord and lead guitar play a fast run in exact unison, virtuosic]
[Episode | shifts into gripping 7/8, tense and technical, double-kick driving]
[Breakbeat | a hard sampled breakbeat drops in and locks in with the live drums, both together]
[Trade | guitar, harpsichord and tapped clean guitar trade solos, faster each time]
[Stretto | all the themes stack on top of each other, maximum density]
[Turn | the harmony swings into D major, the gigue keeps going, triumphant]
[Finale | full band and orchestra, motif hammered out at full speed in D major]
[Outro | one last unison run, the band stops dead together on a single chord]
metadata.gpt_description_prompt:
A gigue closes a Baroque suite and it's fast, compound and joyful. This is the showpiece and the turn in the story: the motif comes back, but now the band plays it, at their tempo, deliberately, hard and fast and on purpose. It isn't gone. It's being played, and this time they're the ones holding the instrument.

Everything on the album gets used here. The 12/8 gallops, there are 7/8 episodes where it grips and slips, there's a proper instrumental slugfest of harpsichord and guitar in unison, and there's a breakbeat that drops in and, for the first time, locks in with the band instead of interrupting. That beat is their own decade, and they're playing along with it instead of being hijacked by it. It ends in D major and it isn't subtle about it.
